source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN Examination, 7th ed.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client with a history of depression is prescribed nadolol for angina. What is MOST important to include when counseling this client?
options: Risk of a fast heart rate
questions.rationale: Beta blockers can worsen depression in clients with a history of it, so these clients are monitored closely. Beta blockers cause bradycardia, not tachycardia.
explanations: Possible, but not the most important point.
Beta blockers can mask hypoglycemia; they do not commonly cause it.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q841 (PDF p. 1078)
questions.quote: Clients with depression or a history of depression have experienced an exacerbation of depression after beginning therapy with beta- adrenergic blocking agents.

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: When should a client take fluoxetine for depression?
questions.rationale: Fluoxetine is taken in the early morning without regard to meals. Taking it later can cause insomnia.
explanations: It must be taken daily, not as needed.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q850 (PDF p. 1087)
questions.quote: Fluoxetine hydrochloride is an antidepressant and is administered in the early morning without consideration of meals.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client with terminal cancer fears becoming addicted to the opioid prescribed for pain. What is the nurse's BEST response?
options: 'Wait as long as you can between doses.'
'Take it only when the pain is very severe.'
'Addiction is rare when opioids are taken for pain.'
'Ask your doctor for a weaker drug.'
questions.rationale: The nurse gives correct information: addiction is rare when medication is taken to relieve pain. Leaving the client in pain is not acceptable.
explanations: Severe pain is harder to control.
Correct: accurate reassurance while keeping pain controlled.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q906 (PDF p. 1149)
questions.quote: Addiction is rare for individuals who are taking medication to relieve pain.

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: A client is admitted with panic disorder. Which benzodiazepine does the nurse expect to be prescribed?
questions.rationale: Alprazolam, a benzodiazepine anxiolytic, depresses the CNS and promotes relaxation in panic disorder. The other drugs are antidepressants.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1004 (PDF p. 1255)
questions.quote: Alprazolam, which is a benzodiazepine antianxiety agent, depresses the central nervous system (CNS) and induces relaxation in clients with panic disorders.

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: A client on imipramine reports increasing drowsiness and fatigue. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: A sign that anxiety is decreasing
A reason to double the dose
questions.rationale: Drowsiness, lethargy, and fatigue on imipramine are adverse effects to report. Expected effects include better appetite and sleep, less anxiety, and a better sense of well-being.
explanations: The dose is never changed by the client.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1011 (PDF p. 1262)
questions.quote: Adverse effects to report to the primary health care provider include drowsiness, lethargy, and fatigue.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client on quinidine for an atrial dysrhythmia misses a dose and remembers 4 hours later. What should the client do?
options: Take the next dose as usual
Stop the drug and call the doctor
questions.rationale: A missed quinidine dose is taken only if remembered within 2 hours; otherwise it is omitted and the normal schedule resumes. Extra or late doses are unsafe.
explanations: Too late; more than 2 hours have passed.
Correct: omit it and resume the usual schedule.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1067 (PDF p. 1349)
questions.quote: the client should be instructed to take the medication if remembered within 2 hours of the missed dose, or omit the dose and then resume the normal schedule.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A transplant client on cyclosporine plans breakfast. Which drink should the client avoid?
questions.rationale: Grapefruit juice blocks cyclosporine metabolism and can raise its levels by 50% to 100%, greatly increasing the risk of toxicity.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1071 (PDF p. 1353)
questions.quote: drinking grapefruit juice can raise cyclosporine levels by 50% to 100%, greatly increasing the risk of toxicity.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which statement shows a client is using a nitroglycerin patch correctly?
options: 'I'll add a second patch if chest pain occurs.'
'I'll put it on a hairless part of my body.'
'I'll rub it in to make it work faster.'
'I'll use it only when I feel chest pain.'
questions.rationale: Topical nitroglycerin is applied to a nonhairy area on a scheduled basis. It is not used specifically for chest pain attacks and is not rubbed in.
explanations: Patches are not added for acute pain.
Correct: apply to a nonhairy area.
Topical nitrates are not rubbed in.
Patches are used on a schedule.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1083 (PDF p. 1365)
questions.quote: Topical nitroglycerin is applied to a nonhairy part of the body.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which instruction is appropriate for a client taking furosemide?
options: Use extra salt in hot weather
questions.rationale: Furosemide is potassium-losing and can cause orthostatic hypotension. The client changes positions slowly, avoids overheating, and discusses alcohol use with the provider.
explanations: Furosemide wastes potassium, so potassium foods are fine.
Correct: heat worsens fluid loss and hypotension.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1084 (PDF p. 1366)
questions.quote: Orthostatic hypotension is a risk, and the client must use caution when changing positions and with exposure to warm weather.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which statement shows a client correctly understands clonidine patch use?
options: 'I'll trim the patch if an edge lifts.'
'I'll take it off whenever I bathe.'
'I'll put it on a hairy area of my chest.'
questions.rationale: The clonidine patch is changed every 7 days and left on while bathing. It is applied to a hairless site and never trimmed, which would alter the dose. A slightly loose patch is covered with the adhesive overlay.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1085 (PDF p. 1367)
questions.quote: The clonidine patch should not be trimmed because it will alter the medication dose.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client is starting cholestyramine for high cholesterol. Which instruction is correct?
questions.rationale: Cholestyramine is taken with food and mixed with water, juice, applesauce, or soup, never dry. Constipation is a common side effect, and fluid intake is increased.
explanations: It must never be taken dry.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1086 (PDF p. 1368)
questions.quote: Cholestyramine must be administered with food to be effective.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client taking colestipol long-term may need supplements of which nutrients?
questions.rationale: Bile sequestrants bind bile salts, interfering with absorption of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K and of folic acid. Long-term users may need supplements.
explanations: Vitamin C is water-soluble and is not affected.
Correct: fat-soluble vitamins and folic acid.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1087 (PDF p. 1369)
questions.quote: the bile salts (which are rich in cholesterol) interfere with the absorption of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K, as well as folic acid.

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: A client on dextroamphetamine has trouble falling asleep. When should the client take the drug?
options: Only on nights of poor sleep
questions.rationale: Dextroamphetamine is a CNS stimulant. Taking it at least 6 hours before bedtime prevents sleep problems. Caffeine should also be avoided.
explanations: Correct: at least 6 hours before bed.
Stimulants do not treat poor sleep.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1092 (PDF p. 1375)
questions.quote: The client should take the medication at least 6 hours before going to bed at night to prevent disturbances with sleep.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client with liver cirrhosis takes triamterene daily. Which finding is an adverse effect of this drug?
questions.rationale: Triamterene is potassium-retaining, so the concern is hyperkalemia, along with dehydration, hyponatremia, and lethargy.
explanations: It causes drowsiness and lethargy instead.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1102 (PDF p. 1386)
questions.quote: Triamterene is a potassium-retaining diuretic. Adverse effects include hyperkalemia, dehydration, hyponatremia, and lethargy.

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of Mother During Labor and Birth
questions.situation: Ate Liza, G1P0 at 41 weeks, is being induced with an IV oxytocin infusion. Nurse Rica is monitoring her closely.
questions.stem: Which contraction pattern shows the oxytocin dose is ADEQUATE?
options: Three to five contractions in 10 minutes, with dilation
Continuous contractions with no rest between
questions.rationale: The goal is the lowest dose that gives 3 to 5 contractions in 10 minutes with cervical dilation. Contractions more often than every 2 minutes reduce their quality and stress the fetus.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1218 (PDF p. 1511)
questions.quote: 3 to 5 contractions in a 10-minute period, with resultant cervical dilation.

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of Mother During Labor and Birth
questions.situation: Ate Liza, G1P0 at 41 weeks, is being induced with an IV oxytocin infusion. Nurse Rica is monitoring her closely.
questions.stem: Which finding should make Nurse Rica suspect water intoxication from the oxytocin?
questions.rationale: Oxytocin has an antidiuretic effect. Signs of water intoxication include tachycardia, dysrhythmias, shortness of breath, nausea, and vomiting.
explanations: Not a sign of water intoxication.
Not a sign of water intoxication.
Not a sign of water intoxication.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1104 (PDF p. 1388)
questions.quote: the woman is monitored closely for signs of water intoxication, including tachycardia, cardiac dysrhythmias, shortness of breath, nausea, and vomiting.

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of the At-Risk and Sick Child
questions.stem: A child with a seizure disorder takes carbamazepine. Which plasma level is in the therapeutic range?
questions.rationale: The therapeutic plasma level of carbamazepine is 5 to 12 mcg/mL. Lower levels may need a dose increase; higher levels risk toxicity.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1127 (PDF p. 1411)
questions.quote: The therapeutic plasma level of carbamazepine is 5 to 12 mcg/mL

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client with heart failure is on long-term diuretics. Which drug puts the client MOST at risk for hypokalemia?
questions.rationale: Bumetanide is a loop diuretic that wastes potassium. Triamterene, spironolactone, and amiloride are potassium-sparing.
explanations: Correct: a loop diuretic causes potassium loss.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1128 (PDF p. 1413)
questions.quote: Bumetanide is a loop diuretic. The client on this medication would be at risk for hypokalemia.

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of Individuals: Communicable & Non-Communicable Diseases
questions.stem: A client on rifampin for TB has new laboratory results. Which finding suggests an adverse effect?
questions.rationale: Rifampin can cause hepatotoxicity, hepatitis, and jaundice. Rising liver enzymes and bilirubin signal an adverse effect.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1130 (PDF p. 1415)
questions.quote: Adverse or toxic effects of rifampin include hepatotoxicity, hepatitis, jaundice, blood dyscrasias

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which statement by a client taking prazosin for hypertension shows a need for more teaching?
options: 'I will skip doses for a few days if dizzy.'
'I will check my blood pressure at home.'
'I will report dizziness to my doctor.'
questions.rationale: Skipping prazosin can cause an abrupt rise in blood pressure. Dizziness and impotence are side effects to report, not reasons to stop on one's own.
explanations: Correct answer: skipping doses causes rebound hypertension.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1131 (PDF p. 1416)
questions.quote: Holding (skipping) medication will cause an abrupt rise in blood pressure.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client with peptic ulcer disease takes large amounts of oral antacids. Which acid-base imbalance should the nurse watch for?
questions.rationale: Excess antacids can cause metabolic alkalosis (pH above 7.45, HCO3 above 27 mEq/L).
explanations: Correct: excess base intake causes alkalosis.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1132 (PDF p. 1417)
questions.quote: when they are taken in excess they can lead to metabolic alkalosis

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client on furosemide and digoxin reports anorexia, nausea, and yellow vision before the morning doses. What should the nurse do FIRST?
questions.rationale: These symptoms suggest digoxin toxicity. The nurse checks the digoxin level first (then potassium, since low potassium worsens toxicity) and holds the drugs until the results are known.
explanations: Furosemide can lower potassium and worsen toxicity.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1176 (PDF p. 1465)
questions.quote: The nurse should check the result of the digoxin level that was drawn because the client’s symptoms are compatible with digoxin toxicity.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which statement shows a client understands how to use sublingual nitroglycerin?
options: 'I'll keep the tablets in my shirt pocket.'
'I'll take one 5 to 10 minutes before activity.'
'I'll keep tablets for several years if unopened.'
'I'll store them in a pill box in the sun.'
questions.rationale: Nitroglycerin can be taken 5 to 10 minutes before an activity that triggers chest pain. It is unstable in heat, cold, and light, so it is not kept close to the body.
explanations: Tablets are discarded 3 to 6 months after opening, by the expiry date.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1213 (PDF p. 1506)
questions.quote: Nitroglycerin may be self-administered sublingually 5 to 10 minutes before an activity that triggers chest pain.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client started betaxolol for hypertension. Which finding shows the drug is having its INTENDED effect?
options: Weight loss of 2 kg in 2 days
questions.rationale: Betaxolol, a beta blocker, lowers blood pressure. Bradycardia, weight gain, and edema are adverse effects that suggest heart failure.
explanations: Edema suggests heart failure, an adverse effect.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1223 (PDF p. 1516)
questions.quote: Betaxolol is a beta-adrenergic blocking agent used to lower blood pressure, relieve angina, or eliminate dysrhythmias.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client takes theophylline, a xanthine bronchodilator. Which drink is the BEST choice?
questions.rationale: Cola, coffee, and chocolate contain xanthines, which add to the cardiac and CNS side effects of theophylline.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1224 (PDF p. 1517)
questions.quote: Cola, coffee, and chocolate contain xanthine and should be avoided by the client who is taking a xanthine bronchodilator.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Misoprostol is added for a client who takes NSAIDs regularly. Which outcome shows it is working?
questions.rationale: Regular NSAID use injures the gastric mucosa, causing epigastric pain. Misoprostol is given to prevent this. Diarrhea is a side effect of misoprostol.
explanations: Diarrhea is a side effect, not the goal.
Correct: it protects the gastric mucosa.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1226 (PDF p. 1519)
questions.quote: The client who regularly takes NSAIDs is prone to gastric mucosal injury, which gives the client epigastric pain as a symptom.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client with AIDS is receiving amphotericin B for a fungal lung infection. Which laboratory finding is an adverse effect?
questions.rationale: Amphotericin B can cause severe hypokalemia (worsened by renal tubular acidosis), leading to muscle weakness and ECG changes.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1230 (PDF p. 1523)
questions.quote: Clients receiving amphotericin B may develop hypokalemia, which can be severe

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client with hyperkalemia receives sodium polystyrene sulfonate. Which serum potassium shows the therapy is effective?
questions.rationale: Normal adult serum potassium is 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L, so only 4.9 is normal. Hyperkalemia causes tall peaked T waves, flat P waves, and a widened QRS.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1236 (PDF p. 1529)
questions.quote: The normal serum potassium level for an adult is 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0 mmol/L).

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client will be discharged once the phenytoin level is therapeutic. Which result meets this goal?
questions.rationale: The therapeutic phenytoin range is 10 to 20 mcg/mL. Lower levels risk seizures; higher levels risk toxicity.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1240 (PDF p. 1533)
questions.quote: The therapeutic range for serum phenytoin levels is 10 to 20 mcg/mL
